title: AI Ethics & Responsible Use — Module Quiz

items.q: The defensibility test asks:
options: How much of the text you typed yourself
Whether you can explain and defend every significant choice
Whether the tool is on an approved list
items.explain: Tool lists are arbitrary and blur constantly. What matters is whether you hold the understanding, not what helped you write it down.

items.q: Why is substituting for assessed work self-defeating?
options: Detection tools are highly accurate
The work is evidence of your understanding, and you end up without it
It always breaches copyright
items.explain: Rules aside, the point of assessment is that you acquire the understanding. Substitution removes the thing you were there for.

items.q: The disclosure test is:
options: Whether an assistant was used at all
Whether the reader would change how they weigh it if they knew
Whether more than half the text was generated
items.explain: Nobody discloses spellcheck because it changes nothing. An assessor weighing your understanding is affected entirely.

items.q: Why is "AI was used in preparing this document" a poor disclosure?
options: It is unnecessarily long
It invites suspicion about everything without saying what to distrust
It admits more than is required
items.explain: Specificity — what was assisted, what you verified — reads as competence and tells the reader where to place weight.

items.q: The argument for disclosing even when nobody requires it:
options: It is always legally safer
The cost is a line; being found out later damages everything else you produced
Readers prefer AI-assisted work
items.explain: The asymmetry does not require professional norms to settle first, and they are genuinely unsettled.

items.q: Why can bias not simply be removed from a model?
options: Providers have not prioritised it
It is entangled with useful patterns, and fairness criteria conflict mathematically
The training data is proprietary
items.explain: Equal error rates, equal predictive value and equal treatment cannot generally all hold at once, so 'make it fair' is underspecified.

items.q: Where does bias most often reach real people in ordinary work?
options: In dramatic, high-profile decisions
In routine sorting, screening and summarising of text about people
Only in image generation
items.explain: Which details survive a summary of a person is a judgement, and it is not made neutrally.

items.q: The most practical bias test for an evaluative task:
options: Ask the model whether it is being fair
Run the same content twice with one identifying detail changed
Use a larger model
items.explain: If the assessment moves when only a name or institution changes, you have learned something essential before relying on it.

items.q: Why can accountability not transfer to a tool?
options: Current law forbids it
It cannot be answerable, cannot be challenged, and cannot put things right
Tools are not yet reliable enough
items.explain: The affected person needs someone who can explain, reconsider and remedy. A model can do none of those.

items.q: Nominal oversight — a reviewer without time or authority — is:
options: Better than no oversight
Worse, because it produces an accountable human who was never in control
Equivalent to real oversight if policy requires it
items.explain: Someone absorbs responsibility for a decision they did not meaningfully make, while the process appears supervised.

items.q: The most useful question for a human reviewing AI output in a decision:
options: Does this output look right?
What would I have concluded if I had not seen this first?
How confident is the model?
items.explain: Automation bias means you defer most when the system is usually right — exactly when a rare error passes unexamined.

items.q: Which is currently the dominant ongoing energy cost for widely-used models?
options: Training
Inference — running the model for every query
Storing training data
items.explain: Training is large and happens once; inference is small per query and enormous in aggregate at present scale.

items.q: Why does cooling water deserve separate mention from electricity?
options: It is more expensive
It is drawn locally, so a datacentre in a water-stressed region is a local issue
It is only used during training
items.explain: Unlike grid electricity, water is a local resource, independent of the grid's carbon intensity.

items.q: The safety filters that make an assistant well-behaved depend on:
options: Automated detection alone
People reviewing harmful material, often outsourced, with documented psychological harm
Rules written by the provider's legal team
items.explain: Making a model refuse the worst things requires people to look at the worst things. That work has been the subject of reporting and litigation.

items.q: Proportionate use means:
options: Using AI as little as possible
Matching the size of the tool to the size of the task
Only using free tiers
items.explain: The largest model is not required to fix a sentence, and choosing a smaller one is the most effective individual action available.

items.q: How does a role usually get hollowed out by automation?
options: Through a formal restructure
Through a series of individually reasonable choices nobody decided together
Through deliberate cost-cutting
items.explain: Each step is sensible on its own, which is why the cumulative effect goes unnoticed until it is finished.

items.q: A task that looks like drudgery from outside may also carry:
options: Only inefficiency
Judgement, relationships, visibility and learning
Nothing worth preserving
items.explain: The person 'just formatting the report' is often catching errors in it, and junior roles are partly how the next senior person is made.

items.q: Why is hiding your own automation a problem?
options: It usually breaches employment terms
The raised output becomes a permanent expectation, and you may never learn the task
Colleagues will find out regardless
items.explain: The new level becomes the baseline, including on the day the tool changes or breaks — and then the knowledge does not exist.

items.q: Why do clear lines collapse in practice?
options: People forget what they decided
The request arrives small, urgent and from someone reasonable, so refusing feels disproportionate
Most such requests are actually fine
items.explain: It never arrives as a proposal to do something wrong. The framing is what makes 'no' feel like an overreaction.

items.q: Which refusal is strongest?
options: "I'm not comfortable with this"
"I can't put unverified figures in a board document — I can have checked ones by Thursday"
"This is against my principles"
items.explain: Comfort is negotiable and sounds like a preference. A specific reason plus the nearest thing you can do separates refusal from obstruction.

items.q: Putting a refusal in writing is primarily:
options: An escalation against the person asking
A record — and often what they need to push back on pressure from elsewhere
A legal requirement
items.explain: A refusal in a searchable channel is a fact; one in a corridor is a disagreement about what was said.

items.q: Why write a personal code in advance rather than deciding case by case?
options: Cases are too varied to judge individually
At the moment of decision you are rushed and want a particular answer
Written rules carry legal weight
items.explain: Consulting a code written calmly honours a judgement you already made under better conditions.

items.q: Which line belongs in a usable code of conduct?
options: "I will use AI responsibly and ethically"
"I will not put a citation in anything I publish unless I have opened it"
"I will be transparent about my methods"
items.explain: The test is whether a line can settle an actual decision. Values commit you to nothing at three in the afternoon.

items.q: Why does a personal code need a review date?
options: To demonstrate compliance
Tools and norms change; unreviewed rules get ignored or obeyed past sense
Codes expire after a year
items.explain: Some rules will look over-cautious later and some naive. Neither gets caught without a date in the calendar.
